title: 1 Samuel 2:27–36
context: A man of God announces judgment on Eli’s house: privilege abused will be removed, Hophni and Phinehas will die on one day, and the LORD will raise up a faithful priest.

verses.text: A man of God came to Eli and said to him, “The LORD says, ‘Did I reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt in bondage to Pharaoh’s house?
verses.arminianNotes: A man of God brings the LORD’s question, “Did I reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt in bondage to Pharaoh’s house?” Arminian readers see God recalling past grace before announcing judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment framed by God’s earlier choice and kindness. The prophetic message begins by reminding Eli of the privileges his family received.

verses.text: Didn’t I choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me? Didn’t I give to the house of your father all the offerings of the children of Israel made by fire?
verses.arminianNotes: God asks, “Didn’t I choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar?” Arminian readers see a privileged calling that brought responsibility to serve faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s sovereign choice of Aaron’s line for priesthood. This verse is mostly shared ground: God’s generous provision makes the sons’ contempt more serious.

verses.text: Why do you kick at my sacrifice and at my offering, which I have commanded in my habitation, and honor your sons above me, to make yourselves fat with the best of all the offerings of Israel my people?’
verses.arminianNotes: God asks, “Why do you kick at my sacrifice and at my offering … ?” and accuses Eli: you “honor your sons above me.” Arminian readers see Eli held responsible for tolerating and sharing in his sons’ abuses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Eli’s failure to honor God above family. The charge “to make yourselves fat” shows that Eli benefited from the corruption he failed to stop.

verses.text: “Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘I said indeed that your house and the house of your father should walk before me forever.’ But now the LORD says, ‘Far be it from me; for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be cursed.
verses.arminianNotes: God says, “… those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be cursed.” Arminian readers see God’s promise conditioned on faithfulness, so the house of Eli forfeits its standing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s faithfulness to his holiness in judging Eli’s house. Readers differ on how such a reversal relates to God’s eternal plan, but the moral principle is shared ground.

verses.text: Behold, the days come that I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, that there will not be an old man in your house.
verses.arminianNotes: God says, “I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house.” Arminian readers see the end of strength and long life for the family as a consequence of its sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a decisive judgment on Eli’s house. The engwebp footnote at “Behold” explains the Hebrew interjection; it is not a textual variant.

verses.text: You will see the affliction of my habitation, in all the wealth which I will give Israel. There shall not be an old man in your house forever.
verses.arminianNotes: “You will see the affliction of my habitation … There shall not be an old man in your house forever.” Arminian readers see judgment that will be felt across generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the lasting consequences of the family’s sin. The verse sets Israel’s prosperity beside the decline of Eli’s house.

verses.text: The man of yours whom I don’t cut off from my altar will consume your eyes and grieve your heart. All the increase of your house will die in the flower of their age.
verses.arminianNotes: The man not cut off “will consume your eyes and grieve your heart,” and descendants will die young. Arminian readers see sorrow as part of the judgment that follows persistent unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the severity of God’s judgment. The engwebp footnote gives “blind your eyes with tears” as an alternative rendering, a translation note rather than a variant.

verses.text: This will be the sign to you that will come on your two sons, on Hophni and Phinehas: in one day they will both die.
verses.arminianNotes: The sign is that Hophni and Phinehas “will both die” in one day. Arminian readers see a clear warning that God’s word will be fulfilled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a sign confirming the certainty of judgment. Its fulfillment is recorded in 1 Samuel 4:11.

verses.text: I will raise up a faithful priest for myself who will do according to that which is in my heart and in my mind. I will build him a sure house. He will walk before my anointed forever.
verses.arminianNotes: God says, “I will raise up a faithful priest for myself who will do according to that which is in my heart and in my mind.” Arminian readers see God’s purposes continuing despite human failure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God providing a faithful servant. Interpreters have identified this priest variously as Samuel, Zadok (see 1 Kings 2:27, 35), or ultimately Christ.

verses.text: It will happen that everyone who is left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread, and will say, “Please put me into one of the priests’ offices, that I may eat a morsel of bread.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Survivors will beg, “Please put me into one of the priests’ offices, that I may eat a morsel of bread.” Arminian readers see a reversal in which those who grabbed food now beg for it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the poetic justice of the judgment. The chapter ends with the house of Eli humbled, echoing the song’s theme of God bringing low the proud.
